quests.instruction: Which layer at the back of your eye catches light and turns it into signals for your brain?
quests.hint: Think of it as the screen at the back of a movie theater.
quests.explanation: The retina is full of cells that sense light. They send signals along a nerve to the brain.
quests.funFact: The picture on your retina is actually upside down, and your brain flips it right side up.

quests.instruction: Which clear, bendy part behind the pupil changes shape to focus on things that are near or far?
quests.hint: A camera has a clear glass part that does the same job.
quests.explanation: Tiny muscles make the lens fatter for close things and let it flatten for faraway things.
quests.funFact: Lenses grow stiffer with age, which is why many grown-ups need reading glasses.

quests.instruction: Which thick cable of nerve fibers carries signals from the back of each eye to the brain?
quests.hint: You have one for each eye.
quests.explanation: The optic nerve carries what the retina senses to the brain, which turns it into the picture you see.
quests.funFact: Each optic nerve holds about a million nerve fibers.

quests.instruction: Deep inside your ear is a tiny, snail-shaped part that turns vibrations into nerve signals. What is it called?
quests.hint: Its name comes from a word for snail.
quests.explanation: Sound vibrations travel through your middle ear into the cochlea, where they are turned into nerve signals for your brain.
quests.funFact: The cochlea is only about the size of a pea.

quests.instruction: Which tiny cells high inside your nose catch scent particles and send smell messages to your brain?
quests.hint: They sit in a small patch at the top of the inside of your nose.
quests.explanation: Scent particles float up your nose and land on smell sensors, which tell your brain what you are smelling.
quests.funFact: People have millions of smell sensors, and a dog has hundreds of millions.

quests.instruction: Which part at the back of your brain helps you keep your balance and move smoothly?
quests.hint: Its name means little brain.
quests.explanation: The cerebellum helps coordinate your muscles, so riding a bike or catching a ball feels smooth.
quests.funFact: The cerebellum is only a small part of the brain's size, but it holds most of the brain's nerve cells.

quests.instruction: Which wide, bumpy back teeth grind food like tiny millstones?
quests.hint: They sit at the back of your mouth.
quests.explanation: Molars have flat, ridged tops that crush and grind food into small pieces.
quests.funFact: Adults can have up to 12 molars, including four wisdom teeth.

quests.instruction: Inside each tooth is a soft center with nerves and tiny blood vessels. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is the part that hurts in a toothache.
quests.explanation: The pulp keeps the tooth alive, and the hard layers around it keep the pulp safe.
quests.funFact: The roots of a baby tooth slowly dissolve as the adult tooth grows in below it, which is why baby teeth get wobbly.

quests.instruction: Which flat, sharp-edged front teeth cut a bite out of an apple?
quests.hint: They are the teeth you see most when you smile.
quests.explanation: Incisors work like little chisels, slicing food into bite-sized pieces.
quests.funFact: People have eight incisors, four on top and four on the bottom.

quests.instruction: Which tiny, disk-shaped cells carry oxygen from your lungs to every part of you?
quests.hint: They give blood its red color.
quests.explanation: Red blood cells pick up oxygen in the lungs and drop it off wherever it is needed.
quests.funFact: A red blood cell lives for about four months.

quests.instruction: The heart has four hollow rooms that fill with blood and squeeze it out. What are they called?
quests.hint: Two are on top and two are on the bottom.
quests.explanation: The upper chambers receive blood, and the lower chambers pump it out.
quests.funFact: The upper chambers are called atria, and the lower ones are called ventricles.

quests.instruction: Which blood vessels carry blood back toward your heart?
quests.hint: Think of them as the return roads.
quests.explanation: Veins bring used blood back to the heart. Arteries carry blood away from it.
quests.funFact: Veins have tiny one-way valves that keep blood from flowing backward.

quests.instruction: Which large organ, tucked under your ribs on the right side, helps clean your blood and makes a juice that helps digest fat?
quests.hint: It is the largest organ inside your body.
quests.explanation: The liver filters blood, stores energy, and makes bile, which helps break down fats.
quests.funFact: The liver can regrow after a part of it is damaged or removed.

quests.instruction: Which stretchy bag stores pee until you are ready to go to the bathroom?
quests.hint: It sits low in your tummy.
quests.explanation: Kidneys make pee, and the bladder holds it until you go. Nerves tell your brain when it is getting full.
quests.funFact: One muscle squeezes the bladder to empty it, and another muscle that you control holds it closed until you are ready.

quests.instruction: Which wide, last part of the digestive tube takes water from the leftovers before they leave your body?
quests.hint: It frames the small intestine like a picture frame.
quests.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water and shapes what is left into waste.
quests.funFact: The large intestine is shorter than the small intestine, but it is wider.

quests.instruction: What smooth, bendy material covers the ends of your bones in a joint and shapes your ears and nose?
quests.hint: It is firmer than skin but bendier than bone.
quests.explanation: Cartilage cushions joints so the bones glide smoothly, and it holds the shape of your nose and ears.
quests.funFact: A shark's whole skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone.

quests.instruction: Which long bone runs from the top of your chest to your shoulder?
quests.hint: You can feel it just below your neck.
quests.explanation: The collarbone holds your shoulder out to the side, so your arm can swing freely.
quests.funFact: The collarbone is among the bones that children break most often.

quests.instruction: Which flat bone in the middle of your chest is where most of your ribs join in front?
quests.hint: You can feel it in the middle of your chest.
quests.explanation: The breastbone, also called the sternum, joins with the ribs to form the front of the rib cage.
quests.funFact: The word sternum comes from the Greek word for chest.

quests.instruction: Heart, blood, and blood vessels work together as which body system?
quests.hint: It keeps blood moving in a loop around your body.
quests.explanation: The circulatory system delivers oxygen and nutrients everywhere and carries waste away.
quests.funFact: Your blood makes a complete trip through this system in about a minute.

quests.instruction: You breathe in air, and oxygen passes into your blood. Which body system makes that happen?
quests.hint: Its main organs are the lungs.
quests.explanation: The respiratory system brings oxygen in and sends carbon dioxide out.
quests.funFact: You take around 20,000 breaths a day.

quests.instruction: I break food into tiny pieces your body can use. I start at your mouth and end at your intestines. What am I?
quests.hint: I include your stomach and your food pipe.
quests.explanation: The digestive system turns food into nutrients that your blood can carry to every part of you.
quests.funFact: Your digestive tube is about nine meters long from end to end.

quests.instruction: Your brain, spinal cord, and nerves make up which system, the body's messaging network?
quests.hint: It sends signals in a split second.
quests.explanation: The nervous system carries messages between your brain and every part of your body, so you can sense, think, and move.
quests.funFact: Laid end to end, all the nerves in an adult would stretch about 70 kilometers.

quests.instruction: Which system, made of muscles and tendons, pulls on your bones to move you?
quests.hint: It lets you run, jump, and smile.
quests.explanation: The muscular system works together with the skeleton to move your body.
quests.funFact: You have more than 600 muscles.

quests.instruction: White blood cells and tonsils team up as which system, protecting you from germs?
quests.hint: It remembers germs it has met before.
quests.explanation: The immune system finds and fights germs, and it remembers them so it can act faster next time.
quests.funFact: Vaccines train the immune system by showing it a harmless piece of a germ.

quests.instruction: Which small flap folds down over your windpipe every time you swallow, so food goes down the right way?
quests.hint: It closes like a little trapdoor.
quests.explanation: The epiglottis covers the windpipe when you swallow, so food slides down the food pipe instead.
quests.funFact: That is why it is wise not to talk or laugh with a full mouth, because food can go down the wrong way.

quests.instruction: Which part of your throat holds the vocal cords that make your voice?
quests.hint: You can feel it move when you swallow.
quests.explanation: The voice box, or larynx, sits at the top of the windpipe. Air passing over the vocal cords makes them vibrate.
quests.funFact: The bump at the front of the neck that some people call the Adam's apple is part of the voice box.

quests.instruction: When you cry, tears drain through tiny tubes into which part, which is why it gets runny?
quests.hint: The tiny tubes start at the inner corner of each eye.
quests.explanation: Tears drain through tiny holes in the inner corners of your eyelids and flow down into your nose.
quests.funFact: Crying for a while can make your nose stuffy because of all the extra tears.

quests.instruction: Which one of these is not part of the digestive system?
quests.hint: It belongs to the system that helps you breathe.
quests.explanation: The stomach and intestines digest food. The lungs belong to the respiratory system.
quests.funFact: Your body has about eleven major organ systems, and they all cooperate.

quests.instruction: A bite of sandwich travels from your mouth to your throat, then down the food pipe. Which part does it reach next?
quests.hint: It is a stretchy bag.
quests.explanation: After the food pipe, food enters the stomach to be mixed with juices.
quests.funFact: Food usually stays in the stomach for about two to four hours.

quests.instruction: Breathing, heartbeat, and swallowing keep going without you thinking. Which part at the base of your brain controls them?
quests.hint: It joins your brain to your spinal cord.
quests.explanation: The brain stem runs the automatic jobs that keep you alive, so you never have to remember them.
quests.funFact: The brain stem is one of the oldest parts of the brain, and many animals have one, too.
